Linux Networking

1. Linux Networking

HarborStatus works when requested on web1, but the administrator cannot reach it from admin1. Reinstalling the web server would change the wrong layer. A request crosses an interface, an address and route decision, network policy, a listening socket, and finally an application. This chapter makes each layer visible before changing any of them.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — Chapter 11 — Linux Networking

2. Trace a request through the network

Name resolution, route selection, transport reachability and correct application content are distinct tests. A successful ping is mistaken for evidence that an HTTPS application works.

SOURCE: Trace a request through the network

3. Chapter 11 — Linux Networking

A request crosses an interface, an address and route decision, network policy, a listening socket, and finally an application. This chapter makes each layer visible before changing any of them.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — Chapter 11 — Linux Networking

4. 11.1 TCP/IP Fundamentals

A network protocol is an agreed way to exchange information. IP delivers packets between addresses. TCP adds a reliable, ordered byte stream between endpoints; UDP sends independent datagrams without TCP’s connection and delivery mechanisms. Applications build their own messages on top. HTTP over TCP, for example, is not the same layer as the IP route carrying it.

Think of an endpoint as an address, transport protocol, and port. TCP port 443 and UDP port 443 are different endpoints. A successful ping does not prove that either accepts an application request. Conversely, a blocked ping does not prove the web service is unavailable. Choose a test that matches the layer and protocol under investigation.

Linux example — 11.1

Observe addresses, routes, and sockets.

What to check: These expose separate TCP/IP layers and do not establish that a remote application works.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.1 TCP/IP Fundamentals

6. 11.2 Network Interfaces

An interface is a network attachment visible to the kernel. It may represent a physical adapter, virtual NIC, bridge, tunnel, or loopback device. Names such as enp1s0 are examples, not portable constants. Identify yours with ip -br link and ip -br address before copying a configuration.

An interface being administratively up does not guarantee a usable physical or virtual link. Read both flags and operational state. A VM can have a functioning guest interface attached to the wrong virtual switch. Trace the interface through the hypervisor rather than treating the guest’s output as the entire network.

Linux example — 11.2

List interface state.

What to check: UP is administrative state; link carrier and usable addressing still need inspection.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.2 Network Interfaces

8. 11.3 MAC Addresses

An Ethernet MAC address identifies a link-layer interface on a local network. IPv4 neighbors commonly resolve an IP address to a MAC address through ARP; IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery. Routers replace link-layer addressing as traffic moves between links, so the remote internet server’s MAC address does not normally appear in your local neighbor table.

Inspect neighbors with ip neigh. An incomplete or failed entry can point toward an unreachable local neighbor, but first confirm that the selected route expects that neighbor on this link. Virtual machines, bonding, and address changes complicate identity. A familiar MAC address is not an authentication mechanism.

Linux example — 11.3

Read MAC addresses from the kernel.

What to check: link/ether identifies Ethernet-style hardware addresses; loopback is different.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.3 MAC Addresses

10. 11.4 IPv4 Addressing

An IPv4 address is 32 bits, usually written as four decimal octets. A prefix length divides the network portion from the host portion. In the teaching subnet 192.168.56.0/24, the first 24 bits identify the network. The remaining eight bits provide address space within it.

A private address does not automatically provide privacy, internet access, or isolation. Those depend on routing and policy. Do not assign a static address merely because it looks unused in one ping test. Check the network allocation record and DHCP pool to avoid duplicate addresses that produce confusing intermittent failures.

Linux example — 11.4

List assigned IPv4 addresses.

What to check: A local address alone does not prove a working gateway or return route.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.4 IPv4 Addressing

12. 11.5 IPv6

IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses. It supports multiple address scopes, including link-local addresses that normally begin with fe80. A link-local destination may need an interface identifier because the same address can exist on different links. Use ip -6 address and ip -6 route to inspect IPv6 separately.

Do not disable IPv6 as a reflexive troubleshooting step. A hostname can return both A and AAAA records, and an application may choose either family. Compare curl -4 and curl -6 where both paths are intended. IPv6 also depends on essential ICMPv6 functions; indiscriminately blocking all ICMPv6 can break normal networking.

Linux example — 11.5

Inspect IPv6 addresses and routes.

What to check: Link-local addresses have a local-link scope and may require an interface identifier.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.5 IPv6

14. 11.6 CIDR and Subnetting

CIDR writes an address followed by its prefix length, such as /24. A longer prefix describes a smaller address range. For ordinary IPv4 broadcast subnets, a /26 has 64 addresses, with conventional network and broadcast reservations leaving 62 host addresses. Special-purpose prefixes, including /31 point-to-point links, require different assumptions.

For 192.168.56.70/26, blocks advance by 64 in the last octet: this address belongs to the block beginning at .64, not .0. Draw the block before choosing a gateway. A mathematically valid address can still violate the organization’s allocation plan.

Linux example — 11.6

Inspect address prefixes.

What to check: The slash suffix is the prefix length; use it to determine the intended subnet boundary.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.6 CIDR and Subnetting

16. 11.7 Default Gateways

A default gateway is the next hop used when no more specific route matches a destination. It is not necessarily the address ending in .1. It must be reachable according to the interface and route configuration, and the router must know how to forward the traffic onward.

The isolated HarborWorks lab interface does not need a default gateway. The separate NAT interface provides outbound access for package downloads. Adding an invented gateway to the host-only interface can divert traffic away from the working NAT path. Preserve the distinction between a local teaching network and an internet exit.

Linux example — 11.7

Read the default gateway selection.

What to check: route get computes a path; it does not send a packet to the documentation address.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.7 Default Gateways

18. 11.8 Routing Tables

Routing selects where a packet goes next. For ordinary destination routing, the most specific matching prefix takes priority; metrics help choose among otherwise applicable routes. Policy routing can add rules based on source and other attributes, so a single default-route line is not the whole story.

Use ip route for IPv4 routes and ip route get 192.168.56.20 to ask how a specific destination would be reached. The latter displays the selected interface and source address without sending a test packet. It is especially useful when a multihomed server replies from an unexpected address. (R26)

Linux example — 11.8

Inspect policy rules and all route tables.

What to check: A route in the main table may not be the one a policy rule selects.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.8 Routing Tables

20. 11.9 DNS

DNS maps names to records; it does not carry the application request after the address is chosen. A server can have perfect routing and still fail by name because its resolver is unavailable or its record is wrong. A correct DNS answer can also point to a service that is down.

Use getent ahosts status.harbor.test to exercise the host’s name-service configuration. Use dig to ask DNS questions directly. These tests are not interchangeable because /etc/hosts, resolver services, search domains, and other name-service sources may affect application lookups. Chapter 13 examines that path in detail.

Linux example — 11.9

Test the configured name-service path.

What to check: getent follows NSS; dig queries DNS. Different results require explaining the configured path.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.9 DNS

22. 11.10 DHCP

DHCP supplies configuration through a lease rather than requiring every address to be entered manually. A lease can include an address, prefix, gateway, DNS servers, and other options. A reservation makes a particular allocation predictable while keeping management centralized.

A client with a lease is not necessarily using the intended configuration: it may have contacted the wrong server or retained old information. Review the network manager’s connection details and logs. Do not start a DHCP server on a shared network for practice; a rogue server can alter other machines’ connectivity.

Linux example — 11.10

On a NetworkManager host, inspect DHCP-derived data.

What to check: Look for DHCP options, gateway, and DNS; static profiles may not have DHCP options.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.10 DHCP

24. 11.11 ip

ip is the main iproute2 interface for inspecting and changing links, addresses, routes, and neighbors. Start with these observations:

A direct ip address add changes kernel runtime state; it does not necessarily update the distribution’s persistent configuration. The network manager may later replace it. Use runtime changes for carefully controlled diagnosis, then implement the approved persistent state through the tool actually managing that interface. (R26)

Linux example — 11.11

Use ip's read-only subcommands.

What to check: Neighbor entries may be incomplete until traffic is attempted.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.11 ip

27. 11.12 ss

ss inspects sockets. sudo ss -lntp shows listening TCP sockets numerically and, where available, owning processes. ss -lun examines UDP listeners. Administrative privileges may be required to identify processes you do not own.

Read the local address as well as the port. 127.0.0.1:8080 is reachable only through local loopback unless another component forwards it. 0.0.0.0:8080 accepts on IPv4 wildcard addresses subject to policy. A listener proves a socket exists, not that requests succeed, and IPv6 wildcard behavior depends on the socket’s configuration. (R26)

Linux example — 11.12

List listening TCP sockets.

What to check: Process attribution may need privilege; listening does not prove firewall reachability.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.12 ss

29. 11.13 ping

ping sends ICMP Echo requests and reports replies and timing. Bound a diagnostic with ping -c 3 ADDRESS; an endless stream is rarely necessary. Start with an intended local neighbor before testing a distant endpoint.

No reply is ambiguous. The destination or an intermediate policy may suppress ICMP, the route may be wrong, or the host may be down. A reply only confirms that this ICMP exchange worked. Pair it with a transport or application test rather than declaring the entire network healthy.

Linux example — 11.13

Bound a reachability probe.

What to check: Loopback success tests a local path; ICMP filtering can make remote ping inconclusive.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.13 ping

31. 11.14 traceroute and tracepath

Route-tracing tools use changing hop limits to reveal some of the path. tracepath is often convenient for an unprivileged investigation; traceroute supports several probe styles depending on implementation. The probes are not identical to every application packet.

A row of asterisks means a response was not received for those probes. It does not necessarily identify the failing router, because devices may filter or rate-limit diagnostic responses while forwarding traffic. Compare paths and times, and avoid attributing blame to the last visible hop without more evidence.

Linux example — 11.14

Probe the path to an approved lab peer.

What to check: Intermediate routers may hide responses; this command is a probe, not a repair.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.14 traceroute and tracepath

33. 11.15 dig

dig NAME A requests IPv4 address records; dig NAME AAAA requests IPv6 records. dig @RESOLVER NAME chooses a particular DNS server. The output’s status, answer section, server, and timing answer different questions. A successful query with no answer of that type is not the same as a timeout.

For the lab, use your actual resolver and configured teaching name. An unconfigured .test name is expected not to resolve through public DNS. Do not publish internal names or query details to external resolvers when organizational policy prohibits that disclosure. (R31)

Linux example — 11.15

Inspect DNS answers and authority data.

What to check: Check status, answer records, and responding resolver; an empty answer can be valid for a record type.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.15 dig

35. 11.16 NetworkManager and nmcli

NetworkManager stores connection profiles and activates them on devices. A profile name is not necessarily an interface name. On the RHEL-family baseline, begin with nmcli device status and nmcli connection show, then inspect the chosen profile before modifying it.

nmcli connection modify changes stored settings; activation applies them and can interrupt SSH. Keep console access and record the previous profile. Never apply an example profile to whichever connection happens to appear first. Ubuntu Server commonly uses Netplan with a networkd renderer instead, so establish the active manager rather than assuming nmcli controls everything. (R27)

Linux example — 11.16

List NetworkManager profiles and device state.

What to check: An existing profile is not necessarily the active profile.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.16 NetworkManager and nmcli

37. 11.17 Static Network Configuration

A static configuration needs a verified address and prefix, plus routes and resolver settings appropriate to that interface. On a dedicated RHEL lab interface, an existing verified profile can be changed to a known unused address such as 192.168.56.10/24 with manual IPv4 addressing and ipv4.never-default yes. The NAT profile remains responsible for the default route.

For an Ubuntu interface managed by Netplan/networkd, the conceptual YAML is:

This is a template, not a file to paste unchanged. Replace the interface, inspect and reconcile existing YAML, preserve the separate NAT configuration, and protect configuration permissions. Validate with sudo netplan generate. Use sudo netplan try from a recoverable console session; its confirmation timeout is useful, but verify rollback actually occurred if it times out. (R28)

Linux example — 11.17

Inspect a verified NetworkManager profile before modifying it.

What to check: Changing a live remote-access profile can disconnect you; use console and rollback for actual edits.

NetworkManager candidate syntax

This illustrative topology must be replaced with your lab settings. Adding a profile is different from activating it; use only the network manager that owns the interface.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.17 Static Network Configuration

41. 11.18 Network Troubleshooting

Work from the request outward: exact source, destination name/address, protocol, port, time, and symptom. Then inspect name resolution, selected route, interface and neighbor state, policy, listener, and application logs. A timeout differs from a connection refusal; a TLS error means the investigation has already reached a later layer.

Change one thing after a test discriminates between hypotheses. Opening every firewall port destroys useful evidence and adds exposure. Record both a positive test from an allowed source and a negative test from a source that should remain blocked.

Linux example — 11.18

Trace a request layer by layer.

What to check: Separate local addressing, routing, resolution, and HTTP/TLS results.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.18 Network Troubleshooting

42. 11.18 Network Troubleshooting · example 1

Work from the request outward: exact source, destination name/address, protocol, port, time, and symptom. Then inspect name resolution, selected route, interface and neighbor state, policy, listener, and application logs. A timeout differs from a connection refusal; a TLS error means the investigation has already reached a later layer.

Change one thing after a test discriminates between hypotheses. Opening every firewall port destroys useful evidence and adds exposure. Record both a positive test from an allowed source and a negative test from a source that should remain blocked.

Linux example — 11.18

Trace a request layer by layer.

What to check: Separate local addressing, routing, resolution, and HTTP/TLS results.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — 11.18 Network Troubleshooting

43. Requirement and simplest approach

admin1 must retrieve HarborStatus from web1 on the isolated lab network. First record the intended address and port. For this exercise, the service will later use TCP 8080. No command in this walkthrough starts a server or changes network policy.

The tempting approach is repeated ping followed by a reboot. Its limitation is that neither identifies whether the application has a socket or whether it listens only on loopback.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — Requirement and simplest approach

44. Selected diagnostic sequence

On admin1, after replacing the example with the verified server address:

On web1:

Interpret the observations as a chain rather than a vote. A route through the correct lab interface plus successful ping establishes useful lower-layer evidence. If ss shows only 127.0.0.1:8080, the remote client’s failure is consistent with an intentionally local listener. If no listener exists, investigate the service before the firewall. If the listener accepts on the expected address, examine host and network policy next.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — Selected diagnostic sequence

48. Verification and recovery

After an approved correction, repeat the exact failed request from admin1, then test the intended negative boundary. Do not call a local curl result proof of remote access. Restore any temporary configuration and verify the expected default route remains unchanged.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — Verification and recovery

49. Practice and implementation lab

Draw the packet path from admin1 to web1. Label which address belongs to each interface and identify the NAT path separately. Predict the effect of accidentally setting a default gateway on the isolated network before experimenting in a disposable VM.

Check your understanding. Does successful ping prove HTTPS works? No. Does editing a NetworkManager profile always apply it immediately? No. Why can getent and dig disagree? They may exercise different name-service paths.

Chapter takeaway. A network failure is a question about a particular path and layer. Test that path, not an undifferentiated idea of “the network.”

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch013.xhtml — Practice and implementation lab

50. Distinguish connectivity from listening service

Layered fixture evidence prevents a route test from becoming an application-health claim. The solution checks the stated outcome explicitly. These fixture results do not establish that a real privileged service is configured correctly.

SOURCE: Distinguish connectivity from listening service
